title: Field notes
intro: Once a week I go through the newsletters I follow on agents, automation and AI tooling and keep the parts a maintenance or operations person could actually use: a sentence or two on the week, then the takeaways, each linked to where it came from.

entries.lede: This week’s thread is trust you can check. The useful advice was about building the check into the system itself: sources you can trace, records that outlast the session, scheduled tests, approval queues and pass or fail gates.

points.t: Make every number traceable. When an AI tool pulls figures or dates from documents, have it cite the file, page and line for each. Then check by type of item rather than a sample of the first few, and always verify money, dates and names against the original.

Organize an AI system around the piece of work, not the persona or the chat session. Keep each job’s history, open items, decisions and next review date in a readable record, so any model or person can pick it up cold.

Per The Headless Brief, providers may lower default reasoning effort or reroute requests under load. Set model and reasoning settings explicitly, and run a scheduled test that sends fixed prompts and confirms the response names the model you asked for.

Replace stop-and-wait approvals with a queue. Let background automation keep working on what it can, gather its decision requests into one structured list, and bring in a person only for the calls that need one.

Control model spend with a pass or fail gate. Send routine tasks to the cheapest model first, test the output against a fixed check such as required fields, and escalate to a costlier model only when the check fails.

entries.lede: This week was about running more than one agent without drowning in them: one front door to ask what needs you, a read-only trial before anything acts, and tight sandboxes and permissions so a stray agent cannot do harm.

points.t: As you add agents, give them one front door: a single place you ask what happened while you were out and what needs you, instead of reading five separate accounts. Teach that coordinator your priorities once, so a change reaches every agent at the same time.

Trial a new automated decision-maker in shadow mode first: feed it a copy of real data, keep it read-only so it cannot touch the live system, and watch its calls on a dashboard before you let it act for real.

Run an autonomous agent in a locked-down sandbox: a non-root user, read-only files, capped memory and no open path to the network. Log what it tries to reach, so a poisoned prompt cannot quietly walk off with your credentials.

A tool connection that can write, not just read, can take real action on its own, like staging a campaign or sending a message. Give each connection the narrowest permissions it needs, and require a human confirmation before anything goes out.

entries.lede: This week the useful thread was where the work really lives and where it waits: keep a job’s state outside the chat, watch for the next place the work piles up, and be honest about what a task actually costs.

points.t: Keep each job’s state in a short plain-text file outside the chat, holding only what the next session needs and stamped with the time. A fresh start, or a nightly reset, then loses nothing, because the note is the memory.

When you speed up one step, the wait just moves to the next one. Look for where your work actually piles up, and turn the review comments you keep repeating into automatic checks the tool runs before a person looks.

Polite words like “please” do not change what a task costs; the number of tokens does. Measure tokens per task if you want to cut the bill, and keep your own timestamped log of what the automation did, separate from the tool that did it.

Agents put work in reach that used to need a team, so the real question is what is worth doing. Judge a new automation by the hours it frees and what those hours are worth, and set a ceiling on what one run may spend before you start it.

entries.lede: This week’s thread was quiet failure: agents that stall without erroring, answers that say “nothing found” when nothing was checked, and the growing need to fence what an agent is allowed to touch.

points.t: Make “couldn’t check” a separate result from “checked, found nothing.” Any scheduled report should list the sources it could not reach; a clean zero only counts when every source answered.
Alarm on silence, not only on errors. A loop that only watches flagged items cannot see the one that went quiet; add a “no update in X hours” check, the same idea as flagging a PM nobody has touched.

Before an agent buys, pays or cancels anything: narrow its access, require an explicit approval for each action, and check the result where it lands (the order, the PO), not in the agent’s own summary.
Give each contributor, human or agent, its own folder and protect the main branch. Changes that stay in scope can be approved automatically; anything else gets a review.
Keep shared work in open formats (Markdown, Mermaid diagrams, plain files) so it survives a change of model or vendor.
